steps.user_message: Here's my situation for 2023 taxes. I'm married filing jointly, live in Portland OR. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $79,400 (W-2). I also earned $22,100 doing graphic design for 3 clients, got $890 interest from Discover Bank savings and $480 dividends from E*TRADE. I work from home in a 100 sq ft office; rent is $2,050/month, total space 850 sq ft. I paid $4,800 in student loan interest (MOHELA, 2018–2019), gave $720 to Northwest Harvest (food bank) have the receipt, and had $780 in work supplies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Here’s how your 2023 federal return likely shakes out and what to use.

What’s deductible
- Self-employment (graphic design):
  - Deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses on Schedule C, including:
    - Home office (see below)
    - Business supplies (if these $780 were for your freelance work)
    - Software/subscriptions, a business share of internet/phone, equipment, mileage, etc. (if applicable)
  - You’ll owe self-employment tax on your net profit (Schedule SE), and you’ll get an above-the-line deduction for half of it.

- Student loan interest:
  - Up to $2,500 above-the-line deduction on Schedule 1 (you paid $4,800, but the max allowed is $2,500).
  - Phaseout for MFJ starts at MAGI $155,000 and ends at $185,000 for 2023—you’re likely under this, so you should get the full $2,500.
  - You should receive Form 1098-E.

- Charitable donations ($720 to Northwest Harvest):
  - Deductible only if you itemize (no above-the-line charitable deduction for 2023).

- Interest and dividends:
  - $890 interest (1099-INT) and $480 dividends (1099-DIV) are taxable. If your total interest and ordinary dividends are under $1,500 and there are no special situations, Schedule B isn’t required, but you still report the amounts.

- Unreimbursed employee “work supplies” ($780):
  - Not deductible for W-2 employee job at the federal level for 2023 (the deduction is suspended through 2025), unless you’re in a narrow exception (e.g., qualified performing artist, Armed Forces reservist, fee-basis government official). If the $780 was for your freelance work, deduct it on Schedule C.

Standard deduction vs. itemizing
- 2023 MFJ standard deduction: $27,700.
- Likely itemizable amounts:
  - State and local taxes (SALT) up to $10,000 cap, plus
  - Charitable $720.
- With rent (no mortgage interest) and typical SALT up to $10,000, your itemized total will likely be well below $27,700. You’ll almost certainly take the standard deduction.
- Note: Taking the standard deduction doesn’t affect your ability to deduct business/home office expenses on Schedule C.

Home office deduction (for your freelance design business)
- You can only claim a home office for your self-employment. Employee home office deductions are suspended.
- Requirements: regular and exclusive use for your business. Using the room for both your freelance work and W-2 work is still “business-only” (no personal use), but you can only deduct against your freelance income.

Two methods:
1) Simplified method
   - $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft.
   - Your 100 sq ft office ⇒ $500 deduction (entered on Schedule C, no Form 8829).
   - No carryforward if limited by income.

2) Actual expense method (Form 8829)
   - Business-use percentage: 100 ÷ 850 = 11.76%.
   - Rent: $2,050/month ⇒ $24,600/year. 11.76% ⇒ about $2,895 deductible as an indirect expense.
   - You can also include a business share of renter’s insurance, utilities, and certain repairs (not provided here), which would increase the deduction.
   - Deduction can’t create/increase a Schedule C loss; unused amount may carry forward.
   - Given your numbers, actual method likely yields a much larger deduction than the $500 simplified method.

Key forms and where things go
- Form 1040
- Schedule 1
  - Student loan interest deduction (up to $2,500)
  - Deduction for half of self-employment tax
- Schedule C (one for your design business)
  - Report $22,100 income (even if you don’t receive 1099s for all clients)
  - Deduct business expenses (supplies, home office, etc.)
  - Home office:
    - Simplified method: enter on Schedule C line 30 using the Schedule C worksheet
    - Actual method: complete Form 8829 and carry the result to Schedule C
- Schedule SE (self-employment tax)
- Form 8995 (QBI deduction)
  - You’ll likely qualify for the 20% qualified business income deduction on your Schedule C profit (below the income threshold for 2023). Software will compute this.
- 1099-INT and 1099-DIV reporting (Schedule B only if required)
- You’ll also file your Oregon return (and any local filings), which have their own rules.

Action items and clarifications
- Please confirm: Were the $780 of “work supplies” for your freelance design business or for your W-2 job? If for freelance, we’ll deduct them on Schedule C.
- Decide on home office method:
  - Actual method likely gives you ≈$2,895 just from rent (more if you add utilities/insurance); requires Form 8829.
  - Simplified is $500 with minimal recordkeeping.
- Keep/collect:
  - 1099-NEC (if any) from clients, or your own records of the $22,100
  - 1098-E for student loan interest
  - 1099-INT from Discover, 1099-DIV from E*TRADE
  - Rent statements and any utility/insurance amounts if using actual method
  - Receipt for the $720 donation

If you want, I can help you choose the home office method and draft a clean checklist of the exact numbers to plug into each form.
